core_principles.title: A Note on Positivity and Practicality
core_principles.description: Being positive is good for both PALS and CALS. It helps us stay strong and hopeful. But at the same time, at least one family member should stay practical when it comes to making important decisions. We can hope that supportive devices will never be needed and still learn about them, discuss them with PALS and plan ahead.

core_principles.title: Using Support Is Not Giving Up
core_principles.description: Equipment can reduce effort and help PALS save energy for the things that matter to them. Needing support does not mean the family has failed.

core_principles.title: You Know the Daily Routine
core_principles.description: You know your PALS best — trust your observations and share them with the doctor. Small changes in sleep, eating or comfort are worth mentioning.

core_principles.title: Look Beyond the Oxygen Reading
core_principles.description: Normal SpO₂ readings can hide CO₂ buildup. Describe symptoms as well as the number on the oximeter.

core_principles.title: Learn from Other Caregivers
core_principles.description: Experienced CALS can help with daily routines, practical preparation and questions to ask. Every PALS journey is different — take guidance but make decisions right for your situation.

key_principles: Plan ahead rather than react to emergencies.
You know your PALS best — trust your observations and share changes with the treating team.
Using support is not giving up. Make daily life easier and save energy for what matters.
Normal SpO₂ readings do not rule out breathing weakness or CO₂ buildup.
Discuss feeding support before meals become exhausting; a PEG does not remove all aspiration risk.
Keep trained help, emergency contacts and tested equipment backups ready.
Learn daily routines from experienced CALS; medicines and machine settings need an individual prescription.
Every PALS journey is different — take guidance but make decisions right for your situation.

categories.name: Respiratory Care & BiPAP
categories.section_note: Plan breathing support before an emergency. Once equipment is advised, arrange it and learn how to use it. Oxygen and an Ambu bag are not automatic requirements for every PALS; they need an individual plan and training.

questions.question: What is BiPAP?
questions.answer:
BiPAP (Bilevel Positive Airway Pressure) is a non-invasive ventilator that helps breathing by providing two pressure levels:

  • Provides higher pressure when breathing IN (IPAP), helps inflate lungs
  • Provides lower pressure when breathing OUT (EPAP), helping keep the airway open
  • Reduces the effort needed from weak breathing muscles. The difference between the two pressures helps move air in and out and clear CO₂
Important: The respiratory team sets the pressures for your PALS. A CPAP machine should not replace prescribed BiPAP support.

sources.label: ALSCAS caregiver perspective: understanding BiPAP and ventilation
NHS: how bilevel ventilation and pressure support work

questions.question: When Does a PALS Need BiPAP, How to Decide?
questions.answer:
Understanding the Core Problem

In ALS, weak breathing muscles may not move enough air in and out. CO₂ (carbon dioxide) can build up, especially during sleep. A pulse oximeter shows oxygen saturation (SpO₂), not CO₂. A normal reading does not mean breathing is necessarily fine.

Signs to discuss with the respiratory team

The Hidden Warning Signs (Even with Normal SpO₂)

  • Cannot sleep at night / frequent position changes - waking up, turning sides many times
  • SpO₂ dropping during deep sleep - check at night, not just daytime
  • Difficulty sleeping flat, needs 2-3 pillows/recliner
  • Morning headaches
  • A persistently faster resting pulse than usual — this can have several causes
  • Daytime drowsiness, fatigue, gasping
  • Breathlessness while eating or talking
  • Faster breathing than usual or a weaker cough
Important: If you notice these changes, contact your doctor or respiratory team and ask about breathing tests and BiPAP. Do not wait for 2–3 signs or a low SpO₂ reading. Severe breathlessness, confusion or difficulty waking needs urgent help.

sources.label: MND Association: support for breathing problems

questions.question: How BiPAP Usage Progresses Over Time? How many hours should PALS use BiPAP daily?
questions.answer:
The Natural Progression

BiPAP usage is not fixed; it may increase as the disease progresses. The key is following the body's needs, not any fixed timeline, with the respiratory team reviewing the plan.

Many PALS start with support during sleep and later need it during naps or in the daytime too. Short daytime practice sessions may help with getting used to the mask. There is no fixed number of hours that suits everyone.

Common Misunderstanding: "Using BiPAP more will make PALS dependent on it faster."

Reality: Needing more support usually reflects changing breathing needs, not a failure caused by using the machine. Do not ration prescribed BiPAP out of fear of dependency.

When PALS asks for more BiPAP time, take that seriously. Tell the respiratory team what has changed; leaks, secretions or an infection may also make breathing harder. If support is needed throughout the day, discuss comfort, backup arrangements and future options. Continuous BiPAP does not automatically mean tracheostomy is needed.

Important: Plan ahead for equipment and training. Once BiPAP is advised, arrange it before you need it urgently, and have a tested power backup.

questions.question: Can early BiPAP help delay tracheostomy?
questions.answer:
Some PALS use BiPAP for a long time without needing tracheostomy. Families understandably want to know how much time it can give them, but there is no fixed number of months or years we can promise.

How Early BiPAP Helps

  • BiPAP gives the diaphragm muscles 'rest' by helping with breathing
  • Less breathing effort can make daily life more comfortable
  • Reduces the work asked of weak breathing muscles
  • Helps clear CO₂ by supporting ventilation
  • Gives families a chance to prepare and review breathing support before a crisis
  • PALS can maintain a better quality of life

To Maximize BiPAP Effectiveness:

  • Ask for a respiratory assessment when breathing symptoms appear
  • Follow the prescribed nighttime plan
  • Get settings and mask fit reviewed by the respiratory team; ask experienced CALS about everyday routines
  • Use suction / cough assist as prescribed and taught for secretion management
Remember: Using BiPAP is not 'giving up'. It is support for breathing and comfort. It does not stop ALS, and different families will have different experiences.

questions.question: When Should we use oxygen concentrator along with BiPAP?
questions.answer:
An oxygen concentrator and BiPAP do different jobs. The concentrator adds oxygen; BiPAP helps move air in and out. Adding oxygen is not a substitute for breathing support.

When oxygen may be needed

A doctor may prescribe it for low oxygen during a chest infection or another lung problem, or for particular comfort needs. Do not start it from a single SpO₂ reading or copy another family’s flow rate.

Before using it at home

  • Write down the prescribed flow, target readings and when to use it.
  • Have the provider show you the correct connection for your machine.
  • Keep the backup supply and emergency contact details ready if oxygen is prescribed.
Important: If breathing worsens or PALS becomes unusually drowsy, seek urgent help rather than turning up oxygen yourself. Oxygen can worsen CO₂ retention in ALS-related breathing weakness. Follow emergency treatment directed by clinicians.

sources.label: MND Association: information for acute and emergency care staff

questions.question: When Is Tracheostomy Needed? What are the decision criteria?
questions.answer:
Understanding the Decision

Tracheostomy is one of the biggest decisions in ALS care. It involves surgically creating an opening in the windpipe (trachea) for direct ventilation, bypassing the nose and mouth entirely.

Planned discussion

This is when you have time to prepare and plan properly. Ask about the options if BiPAP is no longer supporting breathing well, cannot be used comfortably, or secretions are becoming very difficult to clear.

  • What would tracheostomy change for our PALS?
  • What daily suction, ventilation and communication support would be needed?
  • Who will provide care at night, and what training and costs should we plan for?
  • What does PALS want, including if they do not want invasive ventilation?

During an emergency admission

An acute illness may lead to intubation and a discussion about longer-term ventilation. Ask the ICU and ALS teams to explain the choices. Being intubated or using BiPAP 24x7 does not by itself make tracheostomy necessary.

Tip: For tracheostomy, talk to experienced members of the ALSCAS group, talk to as many caregivers as you want. Decision should be yours, your family's, and PALS's together.

sources.label: MND Association: support for breathing problems

questions.question: How to delay or avoid emergency tracheostomy?
questions.answer:
The goal is to prepare early, so that decisions about breathing support can be made with PALS rather than rushed during an emergency.

Practical ways to prepare

  • Arrange BiPAP when advised and use it consistently - Follow the agreed plan and ask for help with mask leaks or discomfort
  • Learn the prescribed suction and cough-assist routine - Oral suction and cough assist have different roles; get hands-on training for the equipment prescribed
  • Discuss PEG early - Do not wait until meals are exhausting or weight loss becomes severe. PEG does not remove all aspiration risk
  • Report signs of a chest infection promptly - Tell the doctor about fever, changed secretions or worsening breathing
  • Good secretion management - Keep the medicines, equipment and routine agreed with the respiratory team ready

Have the essentials ready

  • Arrange prescribed BiPAP before you need it urgently
  • Arrange oxygen or an Ambu bag only if included in the individual plan, with the necessary training
  • Ask whether cough assist would help your PALS
  • Act quickly at first signs of infection - don't wait
  • Have a plan with your doctor and experienced cals for what to do in emergencies
  • Consider home ICU setup for managing care at home
Planning gives you time to prepare mentally, financially, and set up proper home care.
Important: Preparation cannot prevent every emergency. Severe or suddenly worsening breathing difficulty needs urgent help.

questions.question: Why Do Families Delay BiPAP Even After Knowing the Signs?
questions.answer:
Staying positive while being practical

Being positive is essential — it gives strength to both PALS and CALS.

When we are in the caregiver role, we are often overwhelmed with anxiety and fear. We may hope our PALS will never need devices like BiPAP. Even after reading messages and knowing the signs, actually making the decision feels very different — these are new, unfamiliar things that can feel scary.

What seems obvious to those already using BiPAP is not obvious to those facing the decision for the first time. Getting a demonstration and talking to someone who has already managed the mask at home can make it feel less unfamiliar.

This is completely natural. But positivity can sometimes become a barrier to timely action. At least one family member should stay practical when it comes to making important decisions.

Common thoughts that delay the decision:

  • "Our PALS will never need these devices" - but we can hope for the best and still find out how to arrange support if it is needed.
  • "SpO₂ is stable, everything is fine" - but normal SpO₂ can hide dangerous CO₂ buildup and breathing difficulty.
  • "BiPAP might make the muscles weaker or create dependency" - but prescribed support reduces breathing effort; needing more help does not mean the machine caused the illness to progress.

The Reality: Support is there to make breathing easier. Accepting it is not giving up.

Waiting for Doctors to Decide

Do not keep new symptoms to yourself while waiting for the next appointment. Tell the doctor about the broken sleep, extra pillows or morning headaches you are seeing at home. Ask whether breathing muscle tests or overnight checks are needed, even if SpO₂ looks normal.

questions.question: What are HME filters and why are they important?
questions.answer:
HME (Heat and Moisture Exchanger) filters are important for tracheostomy patients:

  • Warm and moisturize the air entering the lungs
  • Help replace some of the warming and humidifying work normally done by the nose and throat
  • Need checking and replacement as instructed; get help promptly if secretions block them or breathing becomes harder

When breathing through a tracheostomy, the air bypasses the nose and throat which normally warm and humidify the air. HME filters help replicate this function, keeping the airways moist and protected.

Important: Use the HME recommended for the exact setup. Not every HME is a bacterial filter, and an HME should not be added to active heated humidification unless the team specifically directs it.

questions.question: When should we consider a feeding tube (PEG)?
questions.answer:
PEG (Percutaneous Endoscopic Gastrostomy) is a feeding tube placed directly into the stomach. The same logic as BiPAP applies here: discussing feeding support early gives you time to prepare. Don't wait for emergencies.

Signs That It's Time to Discuss Feeding Tube

  • Meal takes too long → If eating a normal meal takes more time
  • Difficulty swallowing → Food feels stuck or hard to swallow
  • Coughing or choking while eating or drinking
  • Fear of eating → PALS avoids food because of choking episodes
  • Weight loss
  • Exhaustion after meals → Eating is leaving PALS unusually tired
  • Repeated aspiration → Food may be going into windpipe which can lead to lung infection and emergency

What planning ahead can help with

  • Maintaining nutrition and fluids when eating enough becomes difficult.
  • Taking pressure off long, stressful meals.
  • Giving PALS time to ask questions and decide what they want.
  • Assessing breathing and the safest suitable way to place the tube before a crisis.
Important: A feeding tube does not eliminate aspiration: saliva and reflux can still enter the airway. Plan the timing and method with the specialist team, taking nutrition, breathing and the person’s wishes into account.

sources.label: ALSCAS caregiver guide: swallowing difficulties and feeding tubes
Hull University Teaching Hospitals: PEG benefits and limitations

questions.question: Can PALS still eat by mouth after PEG?
questions.answer:
This is one of the most common concerns. For some PALS, yes — if the swallowing assessment says it is suitable. The tube can take away the pressure of having to meet every nutritional need by mouth.

Having a feeding tube does not automatically mean no oral eating:

  • Some PALS can still have favorite foods by mouth for pleasure, in the texture and amount agreed with their swallowing team
  • The tube can provide nutrition without a tiring full meal, but it does not remove all aspiration risk
  • It may supplement meals or become the main feeding route, depending on swallowing and intake
  • Ask what foods or tastes can be enjoyed safely; the answer can change as swallowing changes
Important: If eating causes coughing, choking or distress, stop and get advice about the feeding plan. Do not assume oral eating is safe just because a PEG has been placed.

questions.question: How to thicken water for PALS with swallowing difficulty (dysphagia)?
questions.answer:
Why thicken liquids?

Water and thin liquids can be difficult to control because they move quickly. A thickener can help some PALS, but the right consistency needs to be worked out with a swallowing therapist.

When to ask for help

  • Coughing or choking when drinking water.
  • Drinks taking longer, being avoided, or leaving PALS tired.

Choosing and using a product

Products mentioned in the caregiver notes include Resource ThickenUp Clear and Thick-It. These are examples to discuss with the therapist, not a recommendation to choose a brand or recipe on your own.

  • Get the required consistency and mixing instructions written down.
  • Follow the instructions for that exact product; a scoop from one brand is not the same as another.
  • Give it the stated time to thicken and check it the way you have been shown.
  • Watch how much PALS actually drinks. A drink that is disliked or hard to swallow can reduce fluid intake.
Important: Do not substitute kitchen xanthan gum without advice. Thickening does not suit everyone or guarantee protection from pneumonia. If swallowing or intake worsens, review the whole feeding plan.

sources.label: RCSLT: thickened fluids and swallowing assessment

questions.recommendation: Consult a speech therapist to determine the right consistency level for your PALS.

questions.question: How can families work with hospital staff during an ALS emergency?
questions.answer:
As CALS, you know the daily routine and the small changes in your PALS. During an ICU admission, that knowledge matters. Explain it to the staff, especially if PALS cannot speak for themselves.

Be prepared to explain the usual care

  • Keep the diagnosis, medicine list and specialist contact numbers together.
  • Write down the usual BiPAP/ventilator settings and hours of use, feeding routine and any prescribed oxygen.
  • Show how PALS says yes or no, calls for help, or uses a communication board.
  • Tell staff if lying flat is difficult, and what has changed from normal at home.
  • Share the person’s care preferences and written emergency plan.

Speak up calmly and firmly

If something does not match the usual care, ask why. You can say, “This is what we normally do at home; could you explain the change?” Ask the ICU team to speak with the treating ALS or respiratory specialist if needed. Do not disconnect equipment or change treatment yourself.

Learn from experienced ALSCAS caregivers, and use that knowledge to ask clear questions. You do not have to stay silent because you are a family member.

Before coming home

Agree on the medicines, equipment, training and help needed for discharge. Keep things simple and written down so that every caregiver can follow the same routine. Home is not automatically safer; come home when the required support is ready.

At home: call and care together

Call 112 immediately in India for severe or worsening breathing difficulty, ineffective ventilation, suspected blocked or displaced tracheostomy, blue/grey colour, collapse or reduced responsiveness. Do not wait for a particular SpO2 reading or try every step first.

One person stays with PALS and provides only trained, prescribed support while another calls emergency services and the treating respiratory/ICU team. If alone, call on speakerphone while staying with PALS.

If external checks and any prescribed, trained suction do not promptly restore effective breathing, stop repeated attempts and obtain urgent skilled help. If the person worsens, escalate immediately. Do not delay help for nebulization or repeated suction cycles.

If a suction catheter will not pass

If the suction catheter will not pass, the TT tube may be blocked or displaced. Call 112 and the respiratory/ICU team now. Do not force the catheter, squeeze an Ambu bag harder, or attempt ventilation through a tube whose patency and position are uncertain.

TT removal/replacement and cuff interventions require a doctor, respiratory therapist or ICU nurse competent and authorized in emergency tracheostomy care. A ventilator technician can help with equipment, but must have specific clinical training and authorization to perform airway procedures. A caregiver should perform an airway intervention only if specifically trained and authorized in that person’s written emergency plan.

Read the emergency escalation guidance.

sources.label: MND Association: information for acute and emergency care staff

questions.question: How Do I Manage Excessive Saliva/Drooling?
questions.answer:
Understanding the Problem

Common Misunderstanding: The body is producing too much saliva.

Reality: Saliva production is often normal. The swallowing muscles have weakened, making it difficult to clear saliva. This causes pooling, drooling, skin irritation, and aspiration risk.

Management Strategies

Active Wiping
Keep a soft cloth handy at all times. Wipe saliva from mouth and face frequently.

Positioning
Find a comfortable supported position. Head elevation or side-lying may help; ask the team to show a position that also works with breathing and feeding.

Oral Suctioning
If oral suction is prescribed, keep the portable machine and Yankauer tip nearby. Use gentle suction as you have been taught. Oral suction is different from deep airway or tracheostomy suction.

Oral Care
Maintain excellent dental hygiene and keep the mouth moist with frequent sips of water (if safe to swallow) or mouth spray to prevent thick, sticky secretions.

Medications (Consult Doctor)
Glycopyrrolate → Reduces secretions (use cautiously, can thicken chest secretions).

Absorbent Products
Keep absorbent bibs or pads handy, and change them when wet.

Dietary Changes
Some families notice a coated or thicker mouth feeling after dairy. Do not cut out useful calories or protein without discussing alternatives with the dietitian.

questions.question: Is glycopyrrolate safe for reducing saliva?
questions.answer:
Understanding the Medication

Glycopyrrolate (also called glycopyrronium) is an anticholinergic that reduces saliva production. It's commonly prescribed for ALS-related saliva management.

Benefits:

  • Reduces saliva production
  • Can significantly decrease drooling

Risks/Side Effects:

  • Thickens chest secretions (major concern in ALS)
  • Dry mouth or throat discomfort
  • Constipation or difficulty passing urine
Important: Use the prescribed product and dose. Keep a short note of whether drooling improves and whether secretions become harder to clear. Report side effects to the doctor; do not copy another family’s dose. New breathing difficulty or inability to clear secretions needs urgent help.

sources.label: NHS: glycopyrronium prescribing and adverse effects

questions.question: How to manage constipation and bowel movements in a bedridden PALS?
questions.answer:
Constipation is very common in ALS due to reduced mobility, medications, reduced fiber/fluid intake, and weak supporting muscles for stool passing.

Start with the daily routine

  • Keep track: note when stool was passed, whether it was hard, and whether PALS was uncomfortable. Share this when caregivers change shifts.
  • Food and feeds: include suitable fruit, vegetables or fibre-containing feeds. Foods discussed in the caregiver notes include papaya, prunes and soaked figs; use textures that fit the swallowing or tube-feeding plan.
  • Fluids: keep up the agreed drinks and feed flushes. The right amount depends on the feeding plan and any heart or kidney restrictions.
  • Regular timing: keep regular meal and toileting times, with a comfortable position and gentle movement where possible.
  • Medicine review: tell the doctor if constipation started after a medicine changed.

When routine measures are not enough

Ask the doctor or pharmacist about a bowel plan before constipation becomes a repeated struggle. Macrogol/polyethylene glycol and lactulose are examples of medicines that may be used. “PEG” here means a laxative, not a feeding tube.

Write down the prescribed dose and when to call if it is not working. Do not choose the medicine or increase the dose just by counting days without stool. Products with similar names can have different ingredients.

Isabgol, suppositories and enemas

Isabgol needs enough fluid and may be unsuitable with swallowing difficulty; do not give it dry or put it through a feeding tube without advice. Use suppositories or enemas only as advised. A plain-water enema is not automatically safer.

Important: Severe abdominal pain, vomiting, a swollen abdomen or inability to pass gas needs urgent assessment. Do not keep adding laxatives or enemas. Medicines can cause cramps, diarrhoea or dehydration; no laxative is guaranteed to be free of side effects.

questions.question: How to prevent bedsores?
questions.answer:
Prevention is Better Than Cure: Bedsores are much easier to prevent than to treat. Once they develop, they can be very difficult to heal.

Prevention steps

  • Use the right mattress: ask which pressure-relieving mattress suits PALS. If it uses a pump, make sure the pump is on and working.
  • Change position regularly: agree a turning schedule with the nurse and write it down. An air mattress does not replace turning; the interval needs to suit the person.
  • Check the skin every day: look at the lower back, buttocks, heels, elbows and under the BiPAP mask. Watch for a patch that stays a different colour, feels hot or firm, or hurts.
  • Keep skin clean and dry: change wet clothing and bedding promptly; use barrier products recommended for the skin.
  • Move gently: use the transfer technique you have been taught instead of dragging PALS across the bed.
Important: If a bedsore develops, consult the nurse or doctor promptly. Do not massage pressure areas or rely on oil, powder or a water cushion to prevent or treat sores. Keep the agreed food and fluid routine going too.

questions.question: Electrolyte Imbalance in PALS - What to Know and How to Manage
questions.answer:
Why this matters at home

If PALS suddenly seems unusually sleepy, weak or unlike themselves, take the change seriously. Electrolytes such as sodium and potassium may need checking, but breathing problems, infection and other illnesses can look similar. Do not assume it is low sodium.

What to keep track of

  • Food, tube feeds and fluids actually taken, including missed feeds or flushes.
  • Vomiting, diarrhoea or changes in urine output.
  • Recent medicine changes, especially diuretics (water tablets).
  • Previous blood-test reports, so the doctor can compare results.

When to ask about blood tests

Agree a follow-up schedule with the doctor. Ask whether a new medicine or an illness means tests are needed sooner. Do not wait for a routine monthly date when PALS is unwell, or treat an abnormal result as their new “normal”.

During diarrhoea or vomiting

Contact the doctor promptly about fluids, feeds and tests. ORS may be advised for some fluid losses; prepare it exactly as directed and check that it fits the swallowing and fluid plan. ORS or coconut water is not a treatment for unexplained drowsiness. Do not add extra salt or potassium to feeds to correct a suspected imbalance yourself.

During a hospital stay

  • Ask about the feeding and fluid schedule; tell staff what PALS normally receives at home.
  • Ask whether electrolyte monitoring is needed, especially if feeds or medicines have changed.
  • Keep copies of results and ask what needs checking after discharge.
Important: Confusion, difficulty waking, seizures, fainting or reduced responsiveness needs immediate medical help. Do not give anything by mouth to someone who cannot swallow safely. Both low and high electrolyte levels can be harmful; treatment depends on blood tests and the cause.

questions.question: What Equipment Do We Need as ALS Progresses?
questions.answer:
ALS needs different equipment at different stages. Get equipment BEFORE you need it urgently. This gives you time to learn how to use it.

These are planning groups, not fixed stages: breathing, mobility and swallowing may change in a different order for your PALS.

For movement and personal care

  • Walker, wheelchair
  • Shower chair, grab bars, raised toilet seat
  • Non-slip mats

For comfort and communication

  • Hospital bed (adjustable height)
  • Pressure-relieving mattress, alongside regular position changes
  • Communication aids (alphabet board, eye tracker)

For breathing support, when advised

  • Prescribed BiPAP machine → arrange it before an emergency
  • Pulse oximeter → know the agreed plan for checking readings and symptoms
  • Suction / cough assist → use the prescribed equipment and get hands-on training
  • UPS/Inverter → power backup is critical
  • Ambu bag → only if part of the emergency plan, with specific training

If PALS has tracheostomy: Confirm ventilation backup, suction and tracheostomy supplies with the provider. An oxygen concentrator and backup cylinder are needed only if prescribed.
questions.recommendation: Don't wait to buy equipment until an emergency. Plan ahead based on changing needs. Rent first, then decide if purchase makes sense.

questions.question: How to Set Up a Home ICU Room for BiPAP + Tracheostomy?
questions.answer:
Setting up a home ICU room needs planning. Keep things simple and organized.

Confirm the exact list with the discharge team: mask BiPAP and tracheostomy ventilation need different setups. Ask them to demonstrate each care task before coming home.

Equipment to organize

CategoryItems
VentilationPrescribed ventilator/BiPAP, compatible circuits and filters, catheter mount and humidification. HME, Whisper Swivel and Ambu bag only if specified for that setup
OxygenOxygen concentrator and backup cylinder, if prescribed
SuctionSuction machine, Vacuum set (Yankauer), Suction catheters, Saline and syringes only for the uses demonstrated by the team
NebulizationCompatible nebulizer and T-piece if prescribed, with the prescribed medicine or sterile solution
MonitoringPulse oximeter, BP cuff, thermometer; multiparameter monitor if advised
Trach CareGauze, gloves, scissors, instructed cleaning supplies and spare TT tubes in the specified sizes
ComfortRecliner bed, Air mattress, Bedside table

Room Setup Tips

  • CCTV camera: use only with consent and controlled access; it does not replace a caregiver
  • PALS comfort: TV, Alexa or AC if wanted; keep the call or communication aid within reach
  • Test equipment: Check all equipment works regularly
  • Keep organized: Have backup supplies ready and easy to find

Backup Items (Always Ready)

CategoryBackups Needed
VentilationSpare TT tubes in the sizes specified by the team, Backup BiPAP/ventilator, Extra circuits & filters
SuctionSecond suction machine, Extra catheters
PowerTested UPS/inverter arrangement; generator only outdoors, away from windows and air intakes
FeedingBackup PEG feeding tube, Syringes
Important: A spare tube is a backup supply, not permission to replace it without training. Keep emergency contacts and written care instructions where every caregiver can find them.

View the Home ICU setup poster and equipment photographs.

sources.label: ALSCAS caregiver checklist: home ICU equipment and room supplies

questions.question: How do I manage if there is a power cut while PALS is on BiPAP or ventilator?
questions.answer:
Power backup is critical for ventilator-dependent PALS. Plan the backup with the equipment provider and electrician, and test the actual runtime before relying on it.

If the power goes out

  • Check that the ventilator has switched to its approved backup and is working. Respond to alarms as trained.
  • If breathing support stops or PALS is distressed, call emergency services and use only the backup method you have been trained to provide.
  • Arrange help or transfer early if the backup will not cover the outage. Do not wait until the battery is nearly empty.
Read our complete guides:
UPS & Power Backup FAQ for Medical Equipment →
Power Backup Calculator & Planning Guide →

questions.question: Will using a power wheelchair or lift make the PALS weaker faster?
questions.answer:
No. This is a common misconception.

ALS affects the nerves that control muscles. Equipment and suitable movement each have a place in care. Conserving energy by using assistive devices—such as a power wheelchair, mechanical lift, or supportive braces—actually helps the PALS maintain energy for essential activities like breathing, swallowing, and communicating.

Key Point: Using support is not giving up. Choose equipment that makes daily life easier, and keep up the movement or exercises advised by the physiotherapist without overdoing it.

Get help with seating, transfers and the right sling for a lift. A wheelchair or lift is for comfort, safety and participation; it is not a treatment that slows ALS itself.
